introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Question 2 : dates de l'historiographie courante (conférence géographique de Bruxelles en septembre 1876, traité de Brazza avec le Makoko en septembre 1880, occupation britannique de l'Égypte en 1882, traité anglo-portugais du 26 février 1884 jamais ratifié, traité de Douala du 12 juillet 1884, conférence de Berlin du 15 novembre 1884 au 26 février 1885) ; aucun chiffre avancé. Le corrigé adopte une position nuancée (le Congo est un déclencheur parmi d'autres causes) : c'est une interprétation, pas un fait.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the view that European rivalry in the Congo prior to 1884 triggered the scramble for African territories in the late 19th century.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The "scramble for Africa" was the rapid partition of the continent by European powers, mainly between about 1880 and 1900. Before 1880 Europeans held only coastal footholds, apart from Algeria, the Cape and a few other areas. The view in the question is that competition between Leopold II of the Belgians, France, Portugal and Britain over the Congo basin in the years before 1884 set off the general rush for colonies. This view is partly correct, because the Congo question led directly to the Berlin West Africa Conference and to new rules for claiming territory. However, it is too simple, because other developments in the same years, notably the British occupation of Egypt in 1882, the French seizure of Tunisia in 1881, the entry of Germany into colonial affairs in 1884 and deeper economic and strategic causes, were at least as important.

**1. The Congo rivalry before 1884.**
- *Leopold II.* After Stanley's journey across the continent (1874-77) the Belgian king hosted the Brussels Geographical Conference in September 1876, which set up the International African Association with humanitarian aims. In 1878-79 he formed the Committee for the Study of the Upper Congo, and, using Stanley, built stations and signed treaties with local chiefs, which led to the International Association of the Congo (1882).
- *France.* Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, working from the Gabon coast, signed a treaty with the Makoko, king of the Teke, in September 1880, giving France a claim on the north bank of the Congo; France ratified it in 1882 and began to compete with Stanley's work.
- *Portugal and Britain.* Portugal claimed the mouth of the river on the basis of old discoveries. Britain, wishing to block France and to protect its trade, signed the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 26 February 1884 recognising Portuguese claims, in return for free trade guarantees. This treaty caused protests from France, Germany, the Belgian king and British merchants, and it was never ratified.
- This rivalry showed that the Congo basin was an area of open competition, and the Anglo-Portuguese treaty led France and Germany to come together; Bismarck then called the Berlin Conference (15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885).

**2. Evidence that the Congo triggered the scramble.**
- The Berlin Conference recognised Leopold's Congo Free State, declared the Congo and the Niger open to free navigation and trade, and laid down the principle of "effective occupation" for new claims on the coast. This encouraged powers to occupy territory quickly in order to secure their claims.
- The conference took place at the moment when other European powers began to claim territory: Germany declared protectorates over Togoland, Cameroon (the treaty with the Duala chiefs of 12 July 1884 and Nachtigal's proclamation), South West Africa and later East Africa in 1884-85, which showed that after the Congo dispute the race had become general.
- The Congo question also gave the imperialist movement in Europe a focus and made colonial annexation fashionable for the public.

**3. Evidence that other factors were equally or more important.**
- *Egypt and North Africa.* The French occupation of Tunisia (1881) and the British occupation of Egypt in 1882, after the Urabi revolt and for the sake of the Suez Canal and the route to India, led to bitter Anglo-French rivalry, so that France turned to West and Central Africa for compensation. Many historians consider that the Egyptian crisis, not the Congo, began the scramble.
- *Economic causes.* The long depression after 1873 made European industrialists look for new markets, raw materials and fields for investment, and the end of the slave trade encouraged interest in tropical products such as palm oil, rubber and groundnuts.
- *Strategic and political causes.* National prestige, the unification of Germany and Italy, the wish to protect sea routes and naval bases, and Bismarck's interest in encouraging Anglo-French rivalry all pushed governments towards colonies; nationalism, popular imperialism and the ideas of civilising and Christianising Africa added to this.
- *Knowledge and technology.* Explorers (Livingstone, Stanley, Barth, Brazza) had opened the interior, and quinine, steamships and breech-loading and later repeating rifles reduced the cost and risk of conquest.
- *Africa itself.* Local rulers' treaties and conflicts such as the dealings of the Duala chiefs with Britain and Germany made it easier for Europeans to intervene.

**4. Evaluation.** Rivalry in the Congo was an important immediate trigger of the Berlin Conference and therefore of the formal rules and pace of partition, but it was one part of a wider crisis. The Egyptian question and European economic and strategic competition had already created the conditions for a partition, and Congo rivalry merely turned them into a quick and open race. It is also worth noting that the Berlin Conference did not itself divide Africa; the actual boundaries were drawn in later bilateral agreements.

**Conclusion.** The view that European rivalry in the Congo before 1884 triggered the scramble for Africa is valid to a limited extent. It explains the timing and procedures of the partition, but not its deeper causes, so it is more accurate to see the Congo dispute as one of several triggers, alongside the Egyptian question, German entry into colonial politics, and the economic and political pressures of the age.
